title: The RBI Will Announce Its Rate Decision Tomorrow. It May Be the Hardest Call Sanjay Malhotra Has Ever Made.
excerpt: With the rupee at record lows, crude oil near $96, and inflation still below target, India's central bank faces a policy dilemma that has no clean answer.
body:
The Reserve Bank of India will deliver its monetary policy verdict on Friday morning, and by the time Governor Sanjay Malhotra steps up to the microphone at 10 AM, he will have navigated one of the most contested rate decisions in recent memory.

The three-day Monetary Policy Committee meeting, which began on June 3, has been conducted against a backdrop that makes every option look inadequate. The rupee has lost 6.5 percent of its value this year, battered by an oil shock triggered by the Iran war and a relentless exodus of foreign portfolio investors who have pulled more than $28 billion out of Indian equities since January. Brent crude sits near $96 a barrel, a price that punishes an economy that imports 90 percent of its oil.

## The case for holding

Nearly 80 percent of 56 economists in a Reuters poll expect the RBI to keep its benchmark repo rate unchanged at 5.25 percent. The logic is straightforward: headline retail inflation remains at 3.48 percent, well below the RBI's 4 percent target. The central bank has already cut rates by 125 basis points through 2025, and the economy needs room to breathe.

"We expect the RBI to hold rates steady, while signalling readiness to respond, should inflation risks intensify and second-round pressures begin to emerge," said Madhavi Arora of Emkay Global Financial Services.

## The case for hiking

But the bond market is telling a different story. Interest rate swaps are pricing in nearly 100 basis points of tightening over the next 12 months, with the one-year OIS rate jumping 65 basis points since March. That is a far more aggressive rerating than anything showing up in government bond yields.

A rate hike could deliver some comfort to the rupee, which briefly touched a record low of 96.96 per dollar before the RBI's aggressive dollar sales and buy-sell swaps pulled it back to around 95.69. But raising rates risks choking growth at a time when monsoon forecasts remain uncertain and global demand is softening.

## The middle path

Rahul Bajoria, chief India economist at Bank of America Global Research, called it "a dilemma of whether to respond to market pressures or incoming data." His recommended path — a hold with hawkish guidance — is the option most analysts consider the least risky. The RBI could keep rates unchanged but shift its stance from "neutral" to "withdrawal of accommodation," signalling that a hike is coming if conditions deteriorate.

## What the RBI has already done

Behind the scenes, the central bank has been anything but passive. Over the past ten days, the RBI has conducted aggressive buy-sell dollar-rupee swaps that have compressed one-year hedging costs from 3.50 percent to 2.92 percent. The forward premium curve suggests the RBI is engineering conditions to cushion the market, regardless of the rate decision itself.

Indian equities ended Thursday flat, with the Nifty 50 up 0.05 percent at 23,416.55 and the Sensex gaining 0.02 percent to 74,360.01. Both benchmarks have lost roughly 2.7 percent over seven sessions. Financials rose 0.3 percent while IT stocks dipped.

## The diaspora stakes

For NRIs watching from abroad, the outcome matters beyond academic interest. A weaker rupee erodes the value of India-denominated assets and remittances. A rate hike makes Indian bonds more attractive but risks slowing the growth that makes India an investment destination. And the broader question — whether the RBI can hold the line on the rupee without sacrificing the recovery — will shape capital allocation decisions for the rest of 2026.

Friday's announcement will not resolve the fundamental tension between a war-driven oil shock and an economy that still needs monetary support. But how Malhotra frames the trade-off will tell markets whether the RBI sees the current stress as temporary or as the beginning of something more durable.
